## The Naive Fix Destroys the Risk {.center}

To carry uncertainty forward, you must **sample**.

. . .

The obvious move — sample each asset on its own — gets every marginal right and
the **joint catastrophically wrong**.

. . .

It can never produce the co-crash. And the co-crash is the risk.

## Independent Sampling Kills the Joint {auto-animate=true}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.8
a, b = datasets.tail_dependent_pair(n=2000, seed=0)
X = np.column_stack([a, b])
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
indep = np.column_stack([rng.permutation(a), rng.permutation(b)])
gen = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, random_state=0).fit(X).sample(2000)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.8))
for ax, data, col, name in [
    (axes[0], X, COOL, f"real · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(a,b):.0%}"),
    (axes[1], indep, CRASH, f"independent · {cocrash_fraction(indep[:,0],indep[:,1]):.0%}"),
    (axes[2], gen, plotting.PALETTE["green"], f"RBIG · {cocrash_fraction(gen[:,0],gen[:,1]):.0%}")]:
    ax.scatter(data[:, 0], data[:, 1], s=6, c=col, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=12); ax.set_xlim(-5, 4); ax.set_ylim(-5, 4)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Identical marginals. Only joint generation keeps the co-crash.

## The Spine — The Same Machine, Backward

$$\underbrace{z = T(x)}_{\text{forward: measure / remove}}
\qquad
\underbrace{x = T^{-1}(z)}_{\text{backward: propagate}}$$

- A map that *simplifies* one way **generates** the other
- Draw $z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$, invert → a real, dependent scenario
- The change-of-variables formula is the recipe: $p_X(x) = p_Z(T(x))\,|\det J|$

## Uncertainty Is a Distribution, Not a Number {auto-animate=true}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
grid = np.linspace(-8, 8, 600)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
ax.fill_between(grid, norm.pdf(grid, 0, 1), color=WARM, alpha=0.35, label="confident (Gaussian)")
ax.plot(grid, student_t.pdf(grid, df=2.5), c=INK, lw=2.2, label="honest (fat-tailed)")
ax.axvline(-4.6, color=CRASH, lw=2, label="realized loss")
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.legend(fontsize=11, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

A point forecast — or a thin Gaussian band — hides the loss that lands in the
tail it never represented.

---

## #2 Gaussian Monte-Carlo — Thin Tails {auto-animate=true}

Fit a covariance, sample a normal. Captures linear co-movement, but Gaussian
tails are **thin** and tail-*independent*.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.4
rng = np.random.default_rng(2); n = 4000
z = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
a2 = 0.5*z + 0.5*rng.normal(0,1,n); b2 = 0.5*z + 0.5*rng.normal(0,1,n)
crash = rng.random(n) < 0.05; shock = np.abs(rng.standard_t(2.5, n)*3.0)
a2 = np.where(crash, a2-shock, a2); b2 = np.where(crash, b2-shock, b2)
D = np.column_stack([a2, b2]); D = (D-D.mean(0))/D.std(0)
gmc = rng.multivariate_normal(D.mean(0), np.cov(D.T), size=n)
pr, pg = D[:,0]+D[:,1], gmc[:,0]+gmc[:,1]
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4))
axL.scatter(D[:,0], D[:,1], s=6, c=COOL, alpha=0.25, edgecolors="none", label="real")
axL.scatter(gmc[:,0], gmc[:,1], s=6, c=CRASH, alpha=0.2, edgecolors="none", label="Gaussian")
axL.set_xlim(-8,4); axL.set_ylim(-8,4); axL.set_xticks([]); axL.set_yticks([])
axL.legend(fontsize=10, frameon=False, markerscale=2); despine(axL)
bins = np.linspace(min(pr.min(), pg.min()), 3, 50)
axR.hist(pr, bins=bins, density=True, color=COOL, alpha=0.55, label="real")
axR.hist(pg, bins=bins, density=True, color=CRASH, alpha=0.45, label="Gaussian")
axR.axvline(np.quantile(pr,0.01), color=COOL, lw=2, ls="--")
axR.axvline(np.quantile(pg,0.01), color=CRASH, lw=2, ls="--")
axR.set_title(f"1% VaR: real {np.quantile(pr,0.01):.1f} vs Gauss {np.quantile(pg,0.01):.1f}", fontsize=12)
axR.legend(fontsize=10, frameon=False); despine(axR)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Same cloud in the middle, **too-optimistic VaR** at the edge.

## #3 RBIG Backward — Keeps the Real Tail

Learn $T$, sample in Gaussian space, invert. The same tool that measured
dependence (Module 1), now a **generator**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6
gen2 = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, random_state=0).fit(D).sample(n)
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, data, col, name in [
    (axL, D, COOL, f"real · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(D[:,0],D[:,1],0.05):.0%}"),
    (axR, gen2, plotting.PALETTE["green"], f"RBIG · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(gen2[:,0],gen2[:,1],0.05):.0%}")]:
    ax.scatter(data[:,0], data[:,1], s=6, c=col, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_xlim(-8,4); ax.set_ylim(-8,4); ax.set_title(name, fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## #4 The Other Uncertainty — Around a Prediction {.center}

So far we sampled the *joint* to price a portfolio. Now: the uncertainty around a
single **prediction** $\hat y = f(x)$.

. . .

Two different questions — two tools, no priors needed:

- **aleatoric** — *how noisy is the world here?* (data noise)
- **epistemic** — *have I even seen data here?* (model doubt)

## Tool A · Predict the Noise {auto-animate=true}

Fit the mean $f(x)$; the **residuals are the noise**. One error bar assumes that
noise is constant — it never is. So fit a *second* model to the squared residuals
→ $\sigma(x)$, and band with $f(x)\pm 2\sigma(x)$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.3
x, y = datasets.heteroscedastic_noise(n=250, seed=0)
mu = np.polyval(np.polyfit(x, y, 5), x)
r = y - mu
sig = np.sqrt(np.clip(np.polyval(np.polyfit(x, r**2, 2), x), 1e-6, None))
const = r.std()
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.3), sharey=True)
axL.fill_between(x, mu - 2 * const, mu + 2 * const, color=CRASH, alpha=0.18)
axL.scatter(x, y, s=10, c=INK, alpha=0.55); axL.plot(x, mu, c=INK, lw=2)
axL.set_title(f"one error bar (constant)  ·  {np.mean(np.abs(r) <= 2 * const):.0%}",
              fontsize=11)
axR.fill_between(x, mu - 2 * sig, mu + 2 * sig, color=COOL, alpha=0.30)
axR.scatter(x, y, s=10, c=INK, alpha=0.55); axR.plot(x, mu, c=INK, lw=2)
axR.set_title(f"predicted σ(x) — breathes  ·  {np.mean(np.abs(r) <= 2 * sig):.0%}",
              fontsize=11)
for ax in (axL, axR):
    ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Same coverage — but the constant bar cries wolf in the calm zone. $\sigma(x)$ puts
the doubt where the world is actually noisy.

## Aleatoric Is Volatility {auto-animate=true}

In markets the noise has a name — **volatility** — and it is *predictable*: it
clusters. Forecast $\sigma_t$ from the recent past (EWMA) and band with
$\pm 2\sigma_t$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.4
R = datasets.load_returns()
r = R["JPM"].to_numpy(); dates = R.index
lam, v = 0.94, np.empty_like(r)
v[0] = np.var(r[:20])
for tt in range(1, len(r)):
    v[tt] = lam * v[tt - 1] + (1 - lam) * r[tt - 1] ** 2  # causal: uses only the past
sig = np.sqrt(v)
cover = np.mean(np.abs(r) <= 2 * sig)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.4))
ax.fill_between(dates, -2 * sig, 2 * sig, color=COOL, alpha=0.35,
                label="±2σ̂  (volatility forecast)")
ax.plot(dates, r, c=INK, lw=0.5, alpha=0.8)
mark_event(ax, pd.Timestamp("2016-06-24"), "Brexit")
mark_event(ax, pd.Timestamp("2018-02-05"), "Volmageddon")
ax.set_ylim(-0.09, 0.09); ax.set_ylabel("JPM daily return")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=11, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The band widens exactly when it must — yet still misses ~7% of days (it should
miss 5%): fat tails. Gaussianize the residuals to close the gap (Module 2).

## Tool B · Ensembles — Does the Model Know?

Refit on resampled data → an **ensemble**. Where the members *agree*, the model is
sure; where they *fan out*, it isn't — and that happens where it has seen no data.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.4
x, y = datasets.heteroscedastic_gap(n=60, seed=0)
xs = np.linspace(-5, 5, 300)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
ens = np.array([np.polyval(np.polyfit(x[i], y[i], 5), xs)
                for i in (rng.integers(0, x.size, x.size) for _ in range(40))])
em, esd = ens.mean(0), ens.std(0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.4))
ax.fill_between(xs, em - 2 * esd, em + 2 * esd, color=plotting.PALETTE["green"], alpha=0.25)
for member in ens[:12]:
    ax.plot(xs, member, c=plotting.PALETTE["green"], lw=0.6, alpha=0.4)
ax.plot(xs, em, c=INK, lw=2); ax.scatter(x, y, s=16, c=INK, zorder=5)
ax.axvspan(-1, 1, color=CRASH, alpha=0.08); ax.set_ylim(-2.2, 2.2)
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Epistemic uncertainty **balloons in the gap**. Add the two:
$\sigma_{\text{aleatoric}}(x)^2 + \sigma_{\text{epistemic}}(x)^2$.

. . .

*(A Bayesian net is the principled limit; a deep ensemble is the cheap, robust
stand-in — same answer, far less machinery.)*

## The Capstone — One Machine, Three Uses {.center}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.0
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 1400
f = rng.standard_t(5, n)
a = 0.85*f + 0.35*rng.standard_t(5, n); b = 0.85*f + 0.35*rng.standard_t(5, n)
Xd = np.column_stack([a, b]); Xd = (Xd-Xd.mean(0))/Xd.std(0)
Z = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, random_state=0).fit_transform(Xd)
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.0))
axL.scatter(Xd[:,0], Xd[:,1], s=6, c=COOL, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
axL.set_title("DATA  (correlated, fat-tailed)", fontsize=12); axL.set_xticks([]); axL.set_yticks([]); despine(axL)
axR.scatter(Z[:,0], Z[:,1], s=6, c=plotting.PALETTE["green"], alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
axR.set_title("GAUSSIAN  (independent, spherical)", fontsize=12); axR.set_xticks([]); axR.set_yticks([]); despine(axR)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**forward** → measure (M1) · remove (M4)    |    **backward** → propagate (M3)

## The Whole Course, One Line {.center}

> Claim only what your evidence justifies.

. . .

The Gaussian is the least-committal joint; what $T$ removes or generates is
*exactly* the dependence in the data.

. . .

**Signal, neutrality, and risk are one operation — read three ways.**
